absent: Locking discipline and ownership of the superblock write guard before tree acquisition and on each failure path.
Behavior of filesystem specific get tree operations and of mount security option enforcement.
Creation, sizing, and destruction of slab caches for mounts, files, backing files, and async contexts.
Implementation of dentry and superblock reference handling including dget, dput, super wake, and locked deactivation.
Final file teardown work routine and delayed work scheduling and execution context.
Private ring file creation, page cache interaction, mapping establishment, and unmapping.
Global async limits tuning and per cpu reference counting lifecycle beyond observed kill and release calls.
Task work infrastructure and RCU work queue ordering and grace period guarantees.
Numeric values of error codes, protection and mapping flags, mount flags, mode bits, and ring magic.

findings.text: Mount construction service that turns a prepared filesystem context into a mount object. On success the caller receives a mount reference and the superblock write guard is no longer held. On failure an error pointer is returned.

Creates a mount from a context that already holds a root. Rejects contexts without a root, allocates a new mount record using the context source name, marks mounts that originate from kernel internal requests, attaches the root, and returns the public mount view or an error pointer on resource failure.

Acquires the mountable root for a context exactly once. Delegates to the filesystem specific tree operation, mandates that a root be present after success, publishes the superblock as born with ordering, applies mount security options, and validates block device linkage and size limits with warnings.

Cleanup helper for a context whose root was acquired but cannot be used, for example after a security failure. Releases the root reference, clears the context root, and deactivates the associated superblock while its lock is held.

Public file reference release. Decrements the reference state and, only when the last reference is dropped, arranges asynchronous teardown through task or delayed work rather than freeing inline in all contexts.

Address space teardown for async state. Visits every context slot of the given memory descriptor, suppresses mapping removal because exit mapping handles it, terminates each live context with a shared completion, waits for in flight work unless all slots were empty, then detaches and frees the table.

Registration service for request cancellation. Ignores control blocks that did not originate from async read or write paths and ignores blocks already queued, otherwise links the request into the context active set and stores the cancel callback under protection.

Small accessor services observed: filesystem option string parsing that tolerates an absent value by passing a null string, inode lookup from a file handle, and container translation between generic file and backing file views with distinct teardown for backing files including credential, path, and cache handling.

Newly allocated mounts satisfy several invariants: a cover object is present, an identifier has been assigned, the device name is never null with a fallback label when no name is supplied, reference counting starts at one logical hold, list and hash membership nodes are initialized, and the mount identity mapping defaults to the null mapping. Any allocation failure unwinds cover, identifier, name, and per cpu state without returning a partial object.

Mount numeric identity is unique within a bounded 31 bit space and carries a separate monotonic unique sequence. Assignment occurs atomically under the identifier map lock so concurrent allocators cannot reuse the same value.

Superblock to mount membership is a singly anchored list with back pointers maintained on insertion. Insertion prepends the new mount and repairs neighbor back links so traversal from the superblock reaches every instance.

Attachment of a root to a fresh mount holds both a superblock active reference and a root dentry reference, designates the root as its own mountpoint and parent, and publishes the instance to the superblock under a read guard.

File teardown path is selected by mode bits: objects lacking both backing and opened markers are freed immediately, accounting is skipped only when explicitly marked, and backing files use a separate cache and release user path state while regular files use the generic file cache.

Ring capacity derivation adds a small overlap margin before page rounding, recomputes usable event count from mapped bytes minus header size, uses an internal folio array up to a fixed threshold and a dynamically allocated array beyond it, and publishes both a kernel trusted count and a user visible header with magic, feature flags, length, identity, and zeroed positions followed by cache maintenance.

System wide async resource use is bounded. Each context records the user requested count for global enforcement while internally doubling and aligning capacity for per cpu distribution. Creation fails when the request exceeds the global maximum or would overflow the global total, and termination subtracts the recorded count under lock with underflow protection.

Available request credits are cached per cpu and refilled in batches. Return of credits accumulates locally and periodically moves a batch to the global counter, while acquisition refills from the global counter with an atomic compare exchange only when the local cache is empty and the global reserve holds at least one batch.

Context lookup by numeric identity uses a dynamically grown table protected for concurrent readers. Insertion reuses the first vacant slot when present. When full, capacity quadruples, existing entries are copied, publication uses release semantics, and the old table is reclaimed after a grace period. Identity stored in the context and in the user ring agree after insertion.

Mount record carries a default null identity map, expiry membership, hash linkage, visibility linkage, hierarchical parent and child relations, sharing and slave relations, cover set membership, tree node linkage, notification queue where enabled, device naming with fallback, cover object, numeric and unique identifiers, reference and writer accounting with per cpu support on multiprocessor builds, superblock association, and sibling linkage for mounts of the same superblock.

Async context record carries a liveness flag, numeric identity with user visible location, mapping size and base, ring file with folio storage in internal and external forms plus page count, event capacity in trusted and user copies, global accounting limit, per cpu credit state with batch size, active request linkage, wait queue, general plus completion plus ring synchronization members, dual reference counts for users and requests, per cpu accounting area, pending destroy waiter, and deferred free work.

Three operation tables are observed for the ring: virtual memory handling that supports remapping plus file backed fault and page operations where memory management is enabled, file handling that only customizes mapping preparation with flags preventing expansion and copying, and address space handling that uses a no operation dirty routine and a migration routine that may be null in some builds.

Mount creation uses an exclusive map guard for identifier assignment, a read guard while publishing a new instance to its superblock, and drops the superblock write guard once tree acquisition succeeds before returning the mount. Identifier map contention is confined to the short allocation window.

Ring folio protection layers distinct concerns: a spin guard around the inode migration pointer defends against teardown, a mutex around ring setup and migration serializes structural changes with nonblocking acquisition during migration, and an interrupt safe completion guard protects the folio pointer swap and content copy from concurrent event production.

Context table mutation holds the memory descriptor table lock while readers use lock free dereference. Remap validation holds the same lock plus a read side critical section while scanning for a matching ring file. Table growth drops the lock during allocation and rechecks identity of the current table before publishing.

Request list and credit paths disable interrupts locally. Cancellation registration and drain of active requests use interrupt safe acquisition of the context guard, while per cpu credit return and acquisition use local interrupt save and restore around counter updates.

Filesystem context progresses from empty to rooted to mounted. Tree acquisition rejects already rooted contexts, delegates to filesystem logic, and on success publishes born state. Security failure discards the root and deactivates the superblock. Mount creation then consumes the rooted context exactly once and releases the superblock guard.

File object release has three outcomes based on execution context and mode. Unopened non backing objects are freed synchronously, normal contexts defer final handling to task work bound to the current thread, and interrupt, kernel thread, or post exit cases queue to a shared delayed list with a scheduled worker.

Async context moves through allocation with ring guard held, table publication and guard release, live use with dual references, termination marking that wakes waiters and unmaps, user reference drain that cancels active requests, request reference drain that waits for in flight work, and deferred reclamation after a grace period that frees ring, counters, and cache.

Folio migration for the ring proceeds only when the inode still references a live context, the ring guard is immediately available, and the source index is within bounds and still current. Mapping migration is followed by a locked copy and pointer replacement, then release of the old folio and guards. Any precondition failure aborts without side effects beyond the reported status.

If the filesystem tree operation reports success without installing a root, the implementation treats this as a fatal programming error because subsequent locking assumptions cannot be recovered. Callers must never allow this state.

Two configuration hazards are reported without failing creation: a superblock lacking block device linkage and a filesystem advertising a negative maximum file size. Both indicate driver defects that should be corrected.

Migration must contend with teardown that clears the inode context pointer, concurrent setup or migration that holds the ring guard, and stale indices caused by prior moves. The code distinguishes permanent rejection from retryable contention to avoid corrupting the folio array or losing events.

Remapping the ring mapping validates file identity, context liveness, and exact size match before updating the user visible base. Mismatched size, dead context, or unknown mapping is rejected, preventing user space from aliasing the ring at an unexpected extent.

Error vocabulary observed: EINVAL for absent root or invalid sizing or unknown folio or mapping, ENOMEM for mount or folio array or table or mapping failures, EBUSY for repeated tree acquisition, EAGAIN for global limit exceeded or contended ring guard or stale folio, EINTR for interrupted mapping lock.

Flag vocabulary observed: SB_KERNMOUNT with MNT_INTERNAL for kernel mounts, FMODE_BACKING with FMODE_OPENED and FMODE_NOACCOUNT for teardown selection, IOCB_AIO_RW for async cancel eligibility, PROT_READ with PROT_WRITE plus MAP_SHARED for ring mapping, VMA_DONTEXPAND_BIT with VMA_DONTCOPY_BIT for ring virtual areas, and AIO_RING_MAGIC with compat and incompat features plus header length for user header validation.

Ring event layout constants derive per page and first page capacities from page size, event size, and header size, with an offset constant capturing the difference between full and first page capacities.
Mount stack entry for filesystems that have completed context parsing. Callable after context holds type and operations. Consumes the context root and yields a mount suitable for attachment.

Teardown entries callable from diverse contexts: file release tolerates interrupt and kernel thread callers by deferring work, while address space exit handles teardown of all async contexts during process exit without unmapping.
